meta.title: Alex Finn: Anthropic has the best model, Grok has the best harness | TWiAI 39
meta.speakers: Jason Calacanis (host), Lon Harris (co-host), Alex Finn, Sarah Hooker, Manu Sharma
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · Fable 5.2 vs GPT-6 Cyber · model vs harness lock-in · Anthropic IPO terms · Nvidia spy story and export controls · anti-data-center politics · Fireworks AI breach

snapshot: Anthropic shipped Fable 5.2 (public) and Mythos 5.2 (vetted cyber/life-science orgs only); OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Cyber, rated **critical** on its own cyber risk tier.
Alex Finn calls Fable 5.2 the best model ever; Sarah Hooker reads the release as a cost story under pressure from open weights ("70% of all traffic").
Calacanis says his team gets more from Grokbot than from Claude and he is weighing dropping Claude; Finn: Claude is the model, Grokbot the best harness.
Anthropic IPO: **$70-78** a share, up to ~$1.405T fully diluted, pricing Nov 18, trading Nov 19 on Nasdaq; ~20% of shares to retail.
Panel split on Jensen Huang after the spy story: Finn and Calacanis say firing him would be a disaster; Manu Sharma questions the timing of the leak.
Hooker and Finn: chip export controls have not worked; Chinese labs rent compute in Southeast Asia. Calacanis expects the Chip Security Act (GPU location tracking) to pass.
Calacanis predicts the anti-data-center movement will be traced to foreign money; Hooker and Finn frame it as public anxiety about AI.

themes.status: FRONTIER RELEASES — TWO LABS, CYBER LOCKED TO VETTED USERS
themes.title: Fable 5.2 and GPT-6 Cyber: breakthrough or cost cut?
themes.lead: Finn sees a real Anthropic breakthrough; Hooker sees a lab cutting cost to justify its premium against open weights.
bullets: Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are the same model per Anthropic, two months after 5.1; Mythos goes only to vetted cyber and life-science orgs.
Fable 5.2 pricing: **$8** per million input tokens, $40 per million output.
GPT-6 Cyber stays in scope **99.93%** of the time vs 94.49% for the prior model, per OpenAI.
Finn: every Anthropic release since Opus 5.5 got smarter, faster and cheaper at once; Fable built a "AAA level" game over two weeks with no input from him.
Hooker: "you don't create a new technique in a month"; enterprises will not move to 5.2 unless it pays off on API bills.
Manu Sharma: no single trick, but RL scaled across many axes; Fable 5.2 steps up in multimodal, science and robot-arm tasks.
Sharma's own company pushes recurring tasks to Sonnet/Haiku-class models and saves the frontier models for long-horizon science and engineering work.

quote.text: Anthropic clearly has had a breakthrough over the last month.

themes.watch: Finn had early access to Fable 5.2 and is building his own agent startup on top of these models.

themes.status: MODEL VS HARNESS — WHO OWNS THE WORKFLOW
themes.title: Claude is the model, Grokbot the harness, and Anthropic wants both
themes.lead: The panel agrees the harness matters as much as the model; it splits on whether Anthropic's lock-in strategy is a strength.
bullets: Calacanis: Grokbot costs **$40** a month per seat (~$10k a year for his team) vs ~$20k a year on Claude with overages; he is considering kicking Claude out.
Finn: "Grokbot is by far the best harness on planet Earth" for knowledge work.
Hooker: Anthropic chose to own model and harness and not co-optimize with third-party harnesses like Hermes; switching is meant to feel a bit painful.
Hooker: the shift to open weights and automated self-improvement makes API lock-in less sticky; that plays out over the next year.
Sharma: enterprise lock-in is strong once IT provisions Claude Cowork with integrations; buyers pick an application (Codex, Grokbot, Claude), not a model.
Calacanis's counter: let each department try two or three tools with a forward-deployed engineer; his team uses Lovable, Claude Code, Grok and Perplexity Computer.

quote.text: They believe that they should own both the harness and the model and it should feel sticky if you try and switch it

themes.title: Anthropic's IPO: priced to $1.4T, but where is the 10x?
themes.lead: The panel expects a strong debut; the open question is how a model lab defends its moat after it.
bullets: Range **$70-78** a share, 825M shares, up to $64.35B raised; up from a $965B valuation in May (CNBC, per Lon Harris).
AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC agreed to buy **$26B** in a private placement at the IPO price.
Calacanis: ~$80B annualized run rate; Anthropic is commoditizing SaaS with Claude Code, design, dashboards, and new whiteboards, sheets and data products.
Finn wants to invest but cannot see a path from $1T to $10T; models can be overtaken overnight, unlike SpaceX's moats.
Hooker: the IPO goes very well; the hard year is after, when Anthropic must move up into legal, tax, healthcare and finance verticals.
Sharma: over **80%** gross margins, no capex (it buys compute), higher compute multiplier; a 2x price cut would lift usage 2-3x.
Harris: Anthropic says 90% of the code for Claude is written by Claude.

quote.text: I just can't envision how does this go from one trillion to 10 trillion.

themes.watch: Finn: frontier labs may only 10x by chasing grand-slam breakthroughs (cancer, disease) because open source eats the consumer side.

themes.status: NVIDIA SPY STORY — INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION UNDERWAY
themes.title: The Nvidia spy story and why export controls already failed
themes.lead: The panel backs Jensen staying, and says chip controls were leaking long before the spy angle.
bullets: The Information: the woman at the centre allegedly helped route at least **$7.5B** in Nvidia chips (~240,000) to two Chinese companies; Reuters could not verify the numbers.
Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe security or company secrets were compromised; outside-counsel investigation underway.
Finn: firing Jensen would be "one of the stupidest things"; founder-CEOs like Jensen and Elon are the company, a hired Google CEO is not.
Sharma doubts the story's timing around the midterms and says intelligence agencies reportedly knew for over a year.
Hooker: export controls were weak regardless; Malaysia, Vietnam and other neighbours host data centers serving Chinese labs, and China is pushing its own chips.
Sharma: Chinese labs do not need chips on the mainland, they can call APIs abroad; he leans toward letting the market decide.
Calacanis: the Chip Security Act (HR 3447) gives Commerce 180 days to require location verification on exported chips; he expects it to pass after this story.

quote.text: I think these chip export controls are much like the drug on war, uh, the war on drugs. It's just not going to work.

themes.watch: All allegations about the woman involved are unresolved; Calacanis repeats a disclaimer on air.

themes.title: Anti-data-center politics: foreign money or real AI anxiety?
themes.lead: Calacanis sees covert funding; Hooker and Finn see a public that fears AI and uses data centers as the symbol.
bullets: A **$5B** data center on the old Landover Mall site in Prince George's County, Maryland is on hold after a 25,000-signature petition and local moratoriums.
Sam Lyman of the Bitcoin Policy Institute links the fight to the Party for Socialism and Liberation; the NPR story does not mention it.
Calacanis predicts much of the movement will be traced to covert foreign money sent through LLCs to "useful idiots".
Hooker: data centers are boring utilities, water use is no worse than a golf course; the real risk is how easily a few citizens can block US infrastructure.
Finn: midterm candidates won on stopping data centers; the fix is education, e.g. free Grok or ChatGPT accounts, not handouts.
Finn's parents went pro-data-center after ChatGPT fixed a broken door they had been quoted **$1,000** for.
Sharma: hyperscalers and local governments must communicate real local benefits with metrics; Harris wants specifics, not Meta's generic El Paso ads.

quote.text: I am going to guarantee and predict right now we're going to do a lot of investigations and find out the anti-data center movement is backed by useful idiots

themes.watch: The foreign-funding link is Calacanis's and Lyman's claim; the panel offers no evidence beyond it.

themes.title: Fireworks AI breach opens a rough six months for cyber
themes.lead: Hooker expects attackers to hold the edge for about six months, pushing companies to keep AI in-house.
bullets: Fireworks AI (hosts and fine-tunes open models for Uber, Shopify, DoorDash) says hackers accessed customer datasets and models over the past month.
Started with misused internal credentials in early October, then a separate attack on **October 24** on R&D machines (Forbes).
Exposed: billing and account info, payment history, parts of unfinished customer models; Fireworks blames LLM-jacking and its CEO says AI agents seemed involved.
Hooker: compute aggregators are more exposed; companies will want fine-tuning on their own premises.

quote.text: It is going to be rough for the next six months until cyber is an adversarial game.

themes.watch: Hooker runs Adaption Labs, which sells self-owned, self-improving fine-tuned models.

takeaways.title: Route recurring work to cheaper models and keep frontier models for long-horizon jobs.
Price the harness, not just the model, before you standardize a team on one vendor.
Watch Anthropic's first year as a public company for vertical moves into legal, tax and finance.
Track HR 3447: GPU location tracking would change how chips are exported and resold.
Audit credentials on any third-party model host holding your data.

hot_takes.take: Grockbot is by far the best harness on planet Earth for just getting pure knowledge work done. Nothing comes close to Grockbot.
you don't create a new technique in a month. This is almost entirely a story about cost.
I think that if Enthropic were to reduce its prices by 2x um the usage would go more than two to 3x um easily.
Elon with all his companies, I think without Elon, any of his companies immediately go to zero.
I'm not buying this story, by the way.

claims.claim: Anthropic prices its IPO Nov 18 and starts trading on Nasdaq Nov 19
A 2x Anthropic price cut lifts usage 2-3x or more
Cyber attackers keep the advantage for about six months
The Chip Security Act (HR 3447) passes after the Nvidia spy story
Much of the anti-data-center movement is traced to covert foreign money
Jensen Huang survives the spy story as Nvidia CEO
